title: Le Ruban Bleu, Herbert Jacobi and the supper club concept
summary: She worked six years at Le Ruban Bleu, an east-side supper club run by Herbert Jacobi, with a new around-the-clock format.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I went into Le Ruban Bleu and stayed there for six years.
That's a club on the east side of New York.
Yeah. That was one of the first supper club in New York on the east side.
Herbert Jacobi, who had come over here from France during the war --
Jacobi had a room in Paris called "Le boeuf sur le toît," in which a lot of the American musicians and acts played there during the better days.
When the war was imminent, you know they began to send all the musicians back. And I happened to be --
In fact, Esquire was doing a montage -- a photographic montage, and I happened to have been

called in because I was new on the scene. They had some Billy Rose -- girl from the Billy Rose cabaret on the cover, and it was a montage.
And Jacobi and Jenny Daniels had just got off the boat more or less. So we wound up in the picture, but that's when I first met Jacobi.
And when he opened Le Ruban Bleu, he opened with Herman Chittison, Dave Barbour, and Cedric Wallace on bass.
And they had around-the-clock entertainment. Usually four acts -- one would go on at a certain time and then they would give intermission.
It was a new concept in the city -- the supper club -- because what he tried to do was arrange it so that mainly it would be the after-theater crowd.
And on top of that, you can call up and find out who was going on at a certain time. If you didn't want to catch the other acts, you could.
And it was more or less a new concept. He brought in some --

You don't mean literally around the clock? You don't mean twenty-four hours?
No, no, no, no. What I mean by that is, the acts didn't go on one right after the other.
They played a set and --
A set and then an act, so that actually -- well we worked until four o'clock in the morning in those days.
But no act went on twice. I usually wound up the last act on the bill, and my first performance would be around twelve o'clock. So, I would say, maybe, every hour.
If you just wanted to come in -- Well the place was small. And they were concerned about turnover. And if you wanted to see somebody special, you just went and caught that act and you left.
